sentences.text: Dubreuillosaurus valesdunensis is the only recognized species of this carnivorous megalosaurid theropod dinosaur.
Physically, the animal was comparable to the dinosaur Eustreptospondylus.
Matthew Carrano identified a unique notch on the rear of the braincase between the basioccipital and the exoccipitals and opisthotic as a distinguishing feature.
The skull was unusually low and elongated, measuring three times longer than it was tall.
The holotype is exceptionally complete, rivaling only Eustreptospondylus in the number of preserved skeletal elements among megalosaurids.
The 2005 paper establishing the new genus included a detailed description of the postcranial skeleton.

Fossils were found in the Calcaire de Caen formation in Conteville, Calvados, France, after the mayor of Conteville, André Dubreuil, noticed bones during land rehabilitation at the Pierre de Caen quarry in 1994.
Professional excavations did not begin until 1998, after the quarry face had already been disturbed by a bulldozer and collapsed rock spread over a considerable surface.
Scientists salvaged approximately two thousand bone fragments ranging from one to ten centimeters in size after sifting through many cubic meters of rubble.
In 2002, before the naming process was complete, Ronan Allain tentatively named the find Poekilopleuron? valesdunensis.
The fossils were found in sedimentary rocks deposited in coastal mangrove swamps along the east coast of the Armorican Massif.
The habitat suggests that Dubreuillosaurus may have hunted fish and other marine prey.
Ronan Allain initially described Dubreuillosaurus as a fish eater, a hypothesis influenced by fish remains found with a related species.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the subadult holotype to be 5 meters long and weigh 250 kilograms, while other estimates indicate the adult could reach up to 9 meters.
Despite living on an island, Dubreuillosaurus did not exhibit insular dwarfism; its small size is attributed to it being a subadult, unlike the adult Eustreptospondylus found in similar settings.

Although the known juvenile specimen lacks crests or horns, it is possible these structures developed as the animal matured, leading to ongoing debate about whether Dubreuillosaurus possessed such ornaments.
Dubreuillosaurus valesdunensis was assigned to Megalosauridae in 2002.
In 2012, Carrano refined this classification to Afrovenatorinae, where it would be the sister species of Magnosaurus, noting the parent group is Eustreptospondylinae.

Dubreuillosaurus was a carnivorous megalosaurid theropod dinosaur that lived during the Middle Jurassic Period, approximately 160 million years ago during the Bathonian stage, from 168.2 to 165.3 million years ago.
During the Middle Jurassic, much of Europe consisted of a series of islands.
A 2024 study by Cau questioned the validity of Dubreuillosaurus, suggesting it is a junior synonym of Poekilopleuron due to individual variation.
